issues.passage: Parking in the fire lane is mandatory under the city’s traffic rules.
issues.why: Uses mandatory correctly to mean required by rules; only world knowledge (fire-lane parking is banned) makes the claim false. A student testing word knowledge would rightly treat this as valid usage.

fix.correctPassage: Safety training is mandatory for everyone who enters the laboratory.
wrongPassages: The handbook labeled the training mandatory so volunteers would know they were free to skip it.
The workshop was mandatory, so volunteers could skip it without consequence.
After a social-media trend, the novel became mandatory among teenagers who simply preferred it.

issues.passage: Driving through a red light is permissible under standard traffic law.
issues.why: Uses permissible correctly to mean allowed under rules; the sentence is only factually wrong about traffic law, not a lexical misuse.

fix.correctPassage: Under the new rules, only certain additives are permissible in the product.
wrongPassages: The handbook called cheating permissible, clarifying that any student caught would be expelled.
Reviewers called the staging permissible, the finest production of the year.
Counsel described the clause as permissible so clients would understand no one was allowed to accept it.

issues.passage: They drafted a permissible contract that neither side could ever revise or cancel.
issues.why: Permissible (= allowed) is used correctly; irrevocability is an extra property, not a misuse of the word. A careful reader can defend this as valid usage.
